title: Strongly coupled quark matter in neutron stars and their mergers
authors: Konstantin Maslov, Ralf Rapp, Joaquin Grefa, Veronica Dexheimer, Claudia Ratti
abstract: The discovery of the strongly-coupled quark-gluon plasma (sQGP) in high-energy heavy-ion collisions has revealed remarkable properties of matter at high temperature, with transport coefficients close to conjectured bounds from quantum field theory at strong coupling. The high sQGP collision rates imply very large energy uncertainties and the melting of quasiparticle structures. Deploying quantum many-body theory based on the self-consistent $T$-matrix approach for the sQGP at high temperature, we investigate its manifestation at high baryon density and low temperature, as present in neutron stars and their mergers. We constrain the chemical-potential dependence of the quark interaction kernel using first-principles information from Quantum Chromodynamics on baryon-number susceptibilities. Very large collisional widths persist at large density and are found to relegate superconducting phases to rather small temperatures. Instead, a strongly coupled diquark liquid prevails in the thermodynamics under the conditions relevant to neutron-star mergers. At lower densities, the diquarks take over from the single-quark contributions, suggesting a pathway toward hadronization. Our results are consistent with observational constraints on the equation of state of neutron stars, corroborating the presence of strongly coupled quark matter in the interior of these objects.
summary: This paper applies advanced quantum many-body theory to model strongly coupled quark matter under the extreme conditions of neutron stars. By extending insights from heavy-ion collisions, the authors predict that the matter in these compact objects is best described as a strongly coupled diquark liquid. The results provide a theoretically consistent Equation of State that aligns with astrophysical observations.
main_problem: The study investigates the properties of strongly coupled quark matter, originally observed in heavy-ion collisions, when subjected to the extreme conditions of high baryon density and low temperature found in neutron stars and their mergers.
main_result: The research predicts that under neutron star merger conditions, a strongly coupled diquark liquid prevails in the thermodynamics, and the resulting Equation of State is consistent with current observational constraints on neutron stars.
method: The authors employ quantum many-body theory, specifically utilizing the self-consistent T-matrix approach derived from the Luttinger-Ward-Baym formalism to calculate thermodynamic potentials.
model_or_system: The system modeled is Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) matter, treating quark-gluon plasma at varying temperatures and baryon chemical potentials. The calculations incorporate interactions via a separable T-matrix approximation.
key_observables: Equation of State (EoS), baryon-number susceptibilities ($\chi_B^{(n)}$), quark pairing instabilities (diquark formation), and the quark self-energy $\Sigma(\omega, p)$.
important_parameters: High baryon density ($\mu_B$), low temperature ($T \approx 3$ MeV), and the comparison to lattice QCD results at $\mu_B=0$.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on the T-matrix resummation technique and the use of a separable interaction model, with the applicability in intermediate density regimes being a noted limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the calibration of susceptibilities against lattice QCD data, the decomposition of pressure into 1-body and correlation contributions, and the analysis of the Thouless determinant to assess diquark condensation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using the T-matrix approach to calculate thermodynamic quantities. It then applies this framework to extrapolate known high-temperature sQGP physics to the high-density, low-temperature regime relevant for compact objects, culminating in EoS predictions.
why_interesting: While focused on QCD, the use of advanced many-body techniques (T-matrix, self-energy calculations) to determine phase structure and thermodynamic stability in a strongly interacting system shares conceptual overlap with modeling correlated quantum fluids or strongly interacting fermionic systems.
